gap: No result ChatGPT got states, in plain terms, that since 27 March 2026 the ICAO rule says a power bank must not be recharged on board and should not be used to charge other devices on board, and that Delta bans charging devices from one during taxi, take-off and landing. So the reason ChatGPT gave for its top pick, charging a laptop from the bank on a long-haul flight, is the one use the rules now discourage or ban.
standout_why: The cited IATA PDF (guidance-to-operators---power-banks.pdf, dated 2026-03-31) appears to contain the rule. Islands.com (Kristin Conard, 2026-09-20) quotes it as power banks 'should not be used to recharge a portable electronic device while onboard the aircraft'. ChatGPT's answer reduced that to '100Wh and two per passenger' plus 'some airlines also restrict using or charging them', and still called a 165 W bank its long-haul laptop pick. The cited American Airlines pages returned 403 to me. RuntimeWise (uncited, result 16) summarises American as 'do not recharge from seat power; keep in reach and visible while in use', so the cited AA page probably covers part of this too. The FAA results (1–8) all returned 403 or were not opened. No rival explains why the rule exists (thermal events) or ties it to how a shopper should pick.
decides: It changes the basis for the pick. While flying, the bank mostly cannot be used: it can't be recharged from seat power, and on ICAO-aligned carriers it shouldn't charge a laptop either. So the high output rating (165–300 W) buys little on the plane. What decides the pick is a printed rating of 100 Wh or less (Delta allows 100 Wh each 'with no exceptions'), stowage under the seat, and enough capacity for layovers and the destination. The page should say 'charge your laptop from seat power and use the bank between flights' rather than 'long-haul laptop bank'. That favours a cheaper 20,000 mAh / 72–74 Wh unit (UGREEN 35524, INIU P62-E1, Baseus Blade H1) over $180–230 300 W banks for flying-only buyers. The Anker Prime 26K's 99.75 Wh also shows that mAh × 3.7 V is not the airline figure. At ChatGPT's 3.7 V it would come to 97.1 Wh, but Anker prints 99.75 Wh, which works out to about 3.8 V. Only the printed Wh counts.

findings.label: ICAO power bank rule: number allowed and in-flight recharging
findings.value: Limited to two per passenger; passengers 'prohibited from recharging them during flights'; effective 27 March 2026
findings.source_title: ICAO: New power bank restrictions will safeguard international aviation
findings.note: ICAO press release dated 27 March 2026. The rule is in the Technical Instructions (Doc 9284). The page gives no Wh figure and doesn't address charging devices.

findings.label: Using a power bank to charge devices on board (UK regulator's wording of the ICAO addendum)
findings.value: 'Must not be recharged on board the aircraft'; 'should not' be used to charge other portable electronic devices on board; maximum two per person
findings.source_title: UK CAA: Changes to rules on the carriage of lithium cells/batteries and power banks
findings.note: Effective 27 March 2026. Over 100 Wh up to 160 Wh still needs operator approval under this text.

findings.label: Why the rule exists (mechanism)
findings.value: 'These restrictions aim to reduce the likelihood and impact of thermal events involving lithium batteries'
findings.source_title: UK CAA: Changes to rules on the carriage of lithium cells/batteries and power banks
findings.note: The UK CAA's stated reason. ICAO's own release says only 'emerging risks'.

findings.label: Delta Air Lines power bank rules
findings.value: Max 100 Wh each 'with no exceptions'; no more than two per person; 'must not be recharged on board'; may not be used to recharge a device during taxi, take-off, landing; not in overhead bin
findings.source_title: Delta Air Lines: Battery or Fuel-Powered Items
findings.note: Result 15 in ChatGPT's list, not cited. 'No exceptions' means a 100–160 Wh bank cannot be approved on Delta.

findings.label: Number of airlines restricting in-flight use or charging (aggregator count)
findings.value: 12 of 15 airline pages read restrict in-flight use or charging; 6 ban both (e.g. Cathay Pacific, Korean Air, Lufthansa Group, Qantas, Singapore Airlines, Emirates)
findings.source_title: RuntimeWise: Airline Power Bank and Battery Rules (2026)
findings.note: RuntimeWise's own count from airline pages (dated 2026-11-05). No rule stated for United, Allegiant or Air Canada. Southwest, Alaska, Spirit, Frontier and Hawaiian pages could not be read.

findings.label: IATA guidance validity and move into the DGR
findings.value: Guidance used with the 67th edition of the IATA DGR, valid through 31 Dec 2026; the 68th edition, effective 1 Jan 2027, puts these updates into the main regulation text
findings.source_title: The Compliance Center: New ICAO Power Bank Addendum Now in Effect
